Thank you, Madam Chair. I just want to thank you guys for letting me take the extra couple of weeks just to review the contract again. And this is obviously a pretty hotbed topic. They're like, "Yes, please." So we're on the last year of this renewal, so has there been a review yet of the performance on this contract thus far? Yes, we review it on a regular basis. Specifically, we meet quarterly with Allied executives to go over the status of the contract and the performance. Okay. And then is that performance ever presented

positively or negatively or whatever? Is any of that feedback provided to the board or the committee at any point in time during the contract? We have not received any such concerns, therefore, no additional

action has been taken. We do not have a process in place like where we report back on any specific contract to the school board other than making you aware if we're issuing and awarding a new contract or doing the renewal. Okay. Thanks. So this is kind of more of a procedural thing. And then I guess what I want to just maybe say and then ask as well, having read this, I think it's just really important for the public to understand that, and as far as I understand, this contract is actually not

really for security per se like our SROs, but it's really more about vestibule and visitor management at our schools, and includes all elementary, middle, and high schools? So the first part of your question is yes, it is all about visitor management. The second part is no, it is not at all middle and high schools. Is it all the elementary? Yes. So all of the elementary and then some of the middle and high schools? Correct. Depending on their staffing needs? Correct.

Okay, because I kind of see this more as like in government terms, we use the phrase staff augmentation. So if the school doesn't have enough people to manage, then we have the Allied folks there. Is that my understanding? Pretty much. Okay. Yeah, there's some nuances involved, but yes. Yeah, I don't need you to get... Yeah. Right. I'm sure there's safety and security issues around that too, which I don't want to disclose, but I just want to... So it's all elementary and then some middle and high schools. Mm-hmm. Okay, great. Thank you so much. Mr. Pepper.

Thank you, Madam Chair. I just want to follow up with Mr. Clark really quickly. When Allied personnel are not present, who handles the visitor management at our schools? That would fall to a front office staff member. Okay. Usually an attendant secretary or someone who's actually an LCPS employee? That's correct. Okay. In addition to their additional roles that they have to handle within the front office, is that correct? Correct. Okay.

Just out of curiosity, and I don't know if you know this off the top of your head because I'm sure it varies greatly, what is the typical number of visitors that perhaps an elementary or middle or high school would get per day? So that's a great question. It varies based on the school. So we have some schools that may get a couple hundred visitors in a six-month period, and others that get in the thousands. It just varies based on the school.

I don't have specific numbers right now, but it does vary widely. Okay, and then last question, I promise. What determines whether a middle or high school qualifies for an Allied security personnel? So it was something that was determined when the contract was first initiated five years ago. And so we have not revisited, we have not added any other positions at the middle and high school level. Do you know what made that determination or not? Okay.

It was a combination of factors. We put out a survey in terms of who needs the support to effectively run visitor management in their school, and so the schools selected did indicate that they needed the support. Thank you. Thank you. I also just wanted to add that I've been speaking to constituents about this. One, in particular, mentioned to me that

why don't we just hire admins that are up at the front to help the staff? Because one of the guards they used to have in this particular elementary school was on the phone the whole time as he walked around and checked doors, was playing on his phone, and just basically checked people in. The other issue is, and I think not as many middle schools have them, correct? It's more so the elementary schools. All the elementary schools have them?

That's correct. I thought they might have been in some of the middle schools. Any middle schools you can think of? No, as I just stated- Yeah ... they are in some middle schools and high schools. They are in some, but about how many? I believe we are in approximately two middle schools at this time. Two. Oh, okay. Yeah, I was actually surprised they weren't in the middle schools. And my understanding is, from one principal I spoke

to, he had mentioned that they don't interview. They come through Allied, they come through you. They had somebody there, it did not work out, and they just decided not to replace the person because they don't interview. So I think that's another issue. Not that you would necessarily look at, but I think that's an issue because maybe, I don't know

if the principal or the staff should have an opportunity to meet with the person first and give you the okay, or hire somebody com-- Well, it would go through Allied, so it would be through you. But that's some of the feedback that I've gotten, that they're on their phones, all they do is check people in. The other issue is sometimes, I think this is rare, that they don't speak English. So as far as that goes,

what are your requirements through the contract to hire some of these people to sit up front? So you've levied a lot of accusations there. So they do have to speak English to work visitor management at a school. Some of the other items that you brought up, you're correct. Principals don't participate in the interview process, and neither do we. They're strictly hired by the contract, in this case, Allied, and that's pretty

standard with contracts of this nature. The contracting company is the one that does the hiring. But as I stated, we meet at a minimum on a quarterly basis to discuss performance, but we are in conversations almost daily with their supervisory chain to address issues like you just brought up. And forgive me, these are just items that were brought up to me when I visit the schools. Mm-hmm. I was just told, I had

no idea. So I just wanted to bring up those items, and thank you for addressing those. And when does this contract need to be renewed again? It'll be effective July 1 once we renew it. So it needs to go through today. It needs to go through this month. Yes. Okay. All right. Thank you. Any other questions? Oh, Mr. Pepper. Yes. Thank you, Madam Chair. And maybe this is for Ms. Willoughby, and I know Ms. Boland is not with us today, because it might be a question for her as well.

And perhaps you know this, because it's really more of a financial question. Do we know what the hourly rate is for one of our, or like an average hourly rate for an administrative assistant of some kind in the front office of a school? For example, not necessarily a principal secretary, maybe like an attendance secretary or someone who would be there. I don't know that off the top of my head. But what I can share is that for LCPS to

have our employees, there's also the additional cost of the benefits. Right. And typically for that level of a position, the cost of the benefits can range from about 30% to 35% of just the salary piece. So that's what also makes those positionsMore costly than perhaps contracting out through a third party. That's kind of where I was headed, so thank you, Ms. Willoughby. And so the other question I have that's kind of a piggyback on that is,

particularly at the elementary level, how many sort of administrative assistants do we have? I know, for example, at my daughter's school, there's, I believe, an attendance secretary, a principal secretary, and perhaps one other. At the elementary school level, we have our staffing standards. And so at a minimum, there would be at least one. And then depending on the size of the school, they may earn additional front office support depending on their size. And they're often doing multiple things like registrar, attendance.

Sometimes they have to juggle multiple roles because of the size of the school. Exactly. Okay. That's why it's typically tiered, even for our secondary schools, that the size of the school typically determines how many additional clerical support positions you have. Appreciate it. Thank you. Any other discussion? Nope? Okay. May I have a motion to approve 5.01? I think... We're just voting, Madam Chair?

So just a little clarification how that number was determined and maybe where we are in the process- Yeah ... and what happens if it still makes sense. So just a little clarification would just be super helpful. Sure. Because I will tell you that I'm not an expert on OPEB. So the 70% funding threshold

basically is indicating that the value of the future benefit that we are responsible for paying for, that we have, in very simple terms, that we've got 70% of the cash in the bank. When we hit that 70% threshold, then we're able to begin making withdrawals from the OPEB funding to pay for the retiree benefits. Right now, it is solely set up as what I would just call a deposit account.

We are just continuously making deposits, and we being Loudoun County, because they make the appropriation directly for our OPEB funding into the OPEB fund. And right now, believe we ended the last fiscal year that we were at about 60%. So we have not reached 70%. The 70% threshold was established, you could say it's a best practice in terms of what a

significant level or sufficient level of funding is. It was a recommendation from our actuary, and then also this is mirrored what the county had in their policy as well. So we were just all being aligned in that manner. So again, once we hit the 70%, then we can have discussions, and we would have discussions at the OPEB Investment Committee with the county staff in terms

of beginning to make withdrawals, and then also perhaps the county not having to continue to make as large as a deposit as they have every year. Right now, they contribute 12 million per year to our OPEB funding. And then eventually, somewhere down the road, once we hit 100%, then they would no longer have to contribute that funding on our behalf. Thank you for explaining the 70% is the best practice.

I think that's the nugget I was hoping to hear. What happens if, say, we get to 70%, we start making the withdrawals, and then we're, say, we're at 72%, then we drop back below the threshold. What happens in that situation? So I believe the recommendation would be that just because we hit 70%... it would not be my recommendation that we ask the county to stop making deposits. We want to really aim for

the 100%. It just gives ourself and the county some flexibility moving forward. This has actually happened with the county where they hit 70%, and they did begin making withdrawals, and then they dipped below, and so then they stopped making the withdrawals and continued to just do deposits only. So that is similar to what we would do if we were to hit above 70%, and we began to make withdrawals, and we dropped below,

then we would stop making withdrawals until we had the sufficient cash in the fund. How would that situation affect our retirees? It does not. It doesn't? It does not. Right now, per our policy, which is a separate policy- Right ... about retiree benefits. This is not what this policy is about. That policy drives what the benefit is that we provide to our retirees. And it's a closed plan,

meaning that anyone hired today, or actually anyone that was hired after, I think, it's 2013 or 2014, they are not eligible for the retiree benefit. It's a closed plan, meaning only for those employees that were hired prior to that date, well over a decade ago, are eligible. So it's easier for us and our actuary to compute what that future value of that benefit is going to

be. And I just lost track of what your question was. I'm sorry. Could you restate? I think you answered that. That was helpful. Okay. So then the other thing was there was a little bit more in there. the goal of fiscal integrity versus adding affordability for all participants. Can you just elaborate on why that doesn't necessarily make sense in terms of this policy, because it's about just funding a pot of money, basically? Exactly. as we administer with HRTD benefits for active and retirees, affordability for our employees and retirees is always one of the top priorities. But sometimes in challenging markets, it can be difficult, as evidenced by we've had several years where we've had to increase our premiums. But it is something that we definitely take into consideration and have as a top priority to try to have a very affordable plan.

Yeah. So like we've said before, this is just about the creation of basically a pot of money and not about how that pot of money is being used. Correct. Thank you. Ms. Record. Thank you so much. conservative. It wouldn't necessarily be we hit 70 or 75. It'd be a more complex analysis and wanting to look at what do the trends look like. So it'd be looking at a number of factors. One just being that that threshold is more of

a green light to begin looking deeper at that in that manner. Okay. And who's doing that analysis? So we have our financial analytics team. That looks at the data. They work collaboratively with human resources and talent development, the benefits team. We also have our Cigna, our insurance providers, as well as our actuary and our consultants. So we have a full team of experts from

different lenses looking at the information. So it's staff, it's Cigna, and the actuaries all looking at it. And then how often are they evaluating?
